answers.answer: The producer publishes an export job ID and inputs; the broker accepts it under its configured durability rules. Confirming that handoff permits an accepted response with job ID and pending status. A worker receives the message, renders and saves the required file and ready status, then acknowledges processing so the broker can retire the delivery. Ready means the file is actually saved, not merely that the broker accepted it. The user must be able to observe failed status if processing later fails. The login decision remains synchronous because access must wait for its result. Operating the broker and workers is one added cost.

evidence.quote: An API must confirm the handoff before telling the client the job was accepted.
Receives the message, saves the required result and ready status, then acknowledges processing to the broker.
Return a job ID and make pending, ready and failed status observable; ready means the required result has actually been saved.
Authorization must finish before granting access to a private resource
The trade-off includes operating the broker and workers

answers.answer: With at-least-once delivery the broker may redeliver after the committed credit and crash before acknowledgement. Acknowledging first risks losing the credit if the worker crashes before saving it. Reuse a stable business-operation ID across attempts. In one database transaction insert that ID into a durable processed-jobs table with a unique constraint and apply the credit: both commit or neither does. A duplicate ID skips the credit; a separate check then write is unsafe because it can race or crash between steps. This protects database effects but does not establish universal exactly-once message delivery or atomic external effects.

evidence.quote: With at-least-once delivery, the broker can deliver the job again.
Acknowledging first instead risks losing the work if the worker crashes before saving it.
Reuse a stable business-operation ID across retries, not a new ID per attempt.
In one database transaction, insert that ID into a durable processed-jobs table with a unique constraint and apply the job's database effect. Commit both or neither. A duplicate ID skips the effect.
It does not make an external email or payment atomic, or turn delivery into a universal exactly-once guarantee.

answers.answer: Retry the temporary image-store outage with increasing delays and a finite attempt or time budget; immediate retries may deepen the outage. On exhaustion isolate the job in a dead-letter queue and expose failed status. An unsupported format will not improve by waiting, so isolate it directly and expose failure. Isolating broken or exhausted jobs lets healthy jobs continue. Before deliberate replay, fix the cause and check whether a prior attempt already applied an effect; replay must retain duplicate safety. The lesson prescribes finite budgets and increasing delays but gives no numeric schedule or budget.

evidence.quote: Retry with increasing delays and a finite attempt or time budget; immediate retries can deepen the outage.
An unsupported input format will not improve with waiting. Isolate it, or any job that exhausts its budget, in a dead-letter queue for investigation and expose failed status.
Healthy jobs can continue. Before deliberately replaying a failed job, fix its cause and check whether an earlier attempt already applied an effect. Replay still needs duplicate safety.

answers.answer: The final quantity may incorrectly be 5: the later event writes 2 first, then the slower earlier event overwrites it with 5. Receiving in order does not ensure completion in order. Serialize effects by item ID, holding later updates while an earlier update runs or retries, while allowing different items in parallel. If the earlier update is dead-lettered, repair or cancel it before releasing dependent updates. A busy item becomes a throughput bottleneck.

evidence.quote: Delivery order and completion order are different.
Serialize effects per entity ID: keep later updates waiting while an earlier one runs or retries. Different entities can still run in parallel. A busy entity becomes a throughput bottleneck.
Moving the earlier job to a dead-letter queue does not resolve the dependency. Decide how to repair or cancel it before releasing dependent updates.

answers.answer: Backlog grows by about 120 - 80 = 40 jobs per second. Increasing oldest-job age means pending jobs are waiting longer and the promised delay may be violated. Keep worker concurrency bounded at the image store safe limit. Throttle or reject producers with a visible busy response, or explicitly defer only within an agreed limit. A queue buffers a burst only if capacity later catches up before finite storage, retention, or allowed delay limits are reached; it cannot solve sustained overload. More workers help when workers are the bottleneck and downstream capacity is spare, which is not the stated image-store situation.

evidence.quote: If 100 jobs arrive each second and 70 finish, unfinished work grows by 30 jobs per second.
Watch backlog and oldest-job age: a growing wait can violate the promise to the client.
Storage and retention are finite. A queue can absorb a burst only if capacity later catches up before those limits or the allowed delay are reached.
Bound worker concurrency to protect the database. Throttle or reject new requests with a visible busy response, or explicitly defer them within an agreed limit.
More workers help when workers are the bottleneck and downstream services have spare capacity.

answers.answer: One work queue distributes jobs among competing workers, so billing and analytics would share jobs rather than each independently receiving every purchase; failed delivery can repeat. A retained log supports separate billing and analytics groups reading the same purchase history independently. Each group tracks an offset for each partition; workers inside a group share partitions. Committing an offset records group progress and does not delete events. Analytics can rewind for a day only if all required events still remain under retention. Partitions are ordered slices, so ordering remains per partition rather than global even with more partitions or consumers. Retained records and offsets do not make external effects universally exactly once.

evidence.quote: A work queue divides jobs among competing workers; it does not give every independent application every job. Failed deliveries can still repeat.
If billing and analytics each need every purchase event, separate consumer groups can track their own progress.
Each group tracks its own position, called an offset, for each partition. Workers within a group share the partitions. Committing an offset records progress; it does not delete the event.

A group can rewind and replay only while the required events remain under the retention policy. Ordering is per partition, not global. Retained history and offsets do not by themselves make external effects exactly once.
